lessons.title: Subprime Loans and the US Housing Bubble

body.text: The 2008 crisis did not begin on Wall Street trading floors. It began with millions of home loans made by lenders who never expected to be holding them when the bills came due.

children.text: This chapter tells the story of the Global Financial Crisis in three parts: the fuse, the explosion and the shockwave that reached India. This lesson is the fuse. You will see how risky American home loans were created, why everyone believed house prices could only rise, and how a chain of institutions passed the risk along until it sat inside banks and funds across the world. Along the way, you will see why India's banks were not holding the same bomb, and how to stress-test a home loan of your own.
What "Subprime" Actually Means

markDefs.definition: A loan made to a borrower with a weak credit history, low or unverifiable income, or high existing debt, who would not qualify for a standard loan. It carries a higher interest rate to compensate for higher default risk.

children.text: A
subprime loan

is a loan to a borrower who would not qualify for a standard, or prime, loan. Lending to riskier borrowers is not wrong in itself, if the lender prices the risk and checks what it can. The problem in the US in the mid 2000s was that checks were abandoned. By 2006, subprime loans made up about 23.5% of all US mortgage originations, according to the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission. Many had features that should have been obvious warning signs.

body.caption: Subprime Loan Features in the US, and How India Handles Them

cells: No Income, No Job, No Assets: loans made with little or no proof of income
Indian lenders typically require income proof such as salary slips or ITRs, plus a CIBIL credit check
Some borrowers financed 95% to 100% of the home's price
RBI caps loan to value at 90% for loans up to ₹30 lakh, 80% up to ₹75 lakh, and 75% above that
A low fixed rate for the first two or three years, then a sharp reset to a much higher floating rate
SBI offered teaser home loans around 2009 to 2011, but RBI discouraged them with a 2% provisioning requirement in late 2010
The lender earned fees and sold the loan, so it did not bear the default risk
Indian banks and housing finance companies have kept most home loans on their own books

children.text: Why Everyone Believed House Prices Could Only Go Up

After the dot-com bust and the 11 September attacks, the US Federal Reserve cut its policy rate to just 1% by June 2003, and held it there for a year. Cheap money made mortgages affordable, rising demand pushed up house prices, and rising prices made lending look safe. US house prices roughly doubled over the boom. A widely held belief took root: national house prices never fall. If a borrower got into trouble, the thinking went, the house could always be sold or refinanced at a profit.

stats.label: US Fed Rate, June 2003
stats.context: The lowest in decades, held for a year

stats.label: US Fed Rate, June 2006
stats.context: After two years of steady increases

stats.label: US House Prices
stats.context: Over the boom, before peaking in 2006

body.title: The Hidden Problem
body.question: Between 2003 and 2006, default rates on many US subprime loans stayed surprisingly low. What best explains this?
options: Subprime borrowers turned out to be as creditworthy as prime borrowers
Rising house prices let struggling borrowers sell or refinance at a profit, hiding how weak the loans really were
US banks had strict income verification rules
The Federal Reserve was paying borrowers' EMIs
body.explanation: While prices rose, a borrower who could not pay simply sold the house or refinanced into a new loan, so the loan never showed up as a default. The weakness was real but invisible. The moment prices stopped rising, that escape route closed, and defaults surfaced all at once. Rising asset prices can make bad lending look good, which is exactly why lenders should not rely on them.

children.text: The Teaser Rate Trap

markDefs.definition: Home loans whose interest rate changes periodically in line with a benchmark rate. A teaser version starts with a low fixed rate for a few years before resetting to a higher floating rate.

children.text: Many subprime borrowers took
adjustable-rate mortgages

with a low teaser rate for two or three years. They qualified based on the teaser payment, not the payment after the reset. When the Fed raised rates from 1% to 5.25% and the teasers expired, monthly payments jumped. To feel the impact, apply the same maths to an Indian home loan using the EMI formula.

body.caption: P is the loan amount, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate divided by 12, as a decimal), and n is the number of monthly instalments.
One ₹40 Lakh Home Loan, 20 Year Tenure: What a Reset Does to the EMI

children.text: A family that could just about manage ₹32,224 a month suddenly owes ₹39,935 or more, with no increase in income. In the US, millions of borrowers hit this wall between 2006 and 2008. In India, floating rate borrowers usually see their loan tenure extended first when rates rise, rather than an immediate EMI jump, which softens the shock but makes the loan far more expensive over its life.

body.title: Your Turn: Stress-Test a Teaser Loan
body.prompt: Use the EMI calculator above. Sneha takes a ₹30 lakh home loan for 15 years at a teaser rate of 8%. After the teaser period, the rate resets to 11%. Assuming the EMI is recalculated over the same 15 years, by what percentage does her EMI rise? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: At 8%, the EMI is about ₹28,670. At 11%, it is about ₹34,098. That is an increase of about 18.9%. If Sneha's EMI was already 40% of her take-home pay, it would jump to roughly 48% of her pay overnight. (For simplicity, this recalculates the EMI on the original loan over the full tenure; a real reset would apply to the outstanding balance and remaining tenure.)

children.text: The Securitisation Machine

markDefs.definition: A lending model where the lender makes loans in order to sell them on to other investors, earning fees on volume rather than bearing the long-term risk of default.
Bonds backed by a pool of home loans. Investors receive the interest and principal payments that borrowers make on the underlying loans.
Pooling loans or other cash-generating assets and turning them into tradable securities sold to investors.

children.text: In traditional lending, a bank that makes a loan keeps it and cares whether it is repaid. In the US housing boom, most subprime loans followed a different model, called
originate to distribute
. Lenders sold the loans to investment banks, which bundled thousands of them into
mortgage-backed securities (MBS)
through a process called
securitisation
. Some of these securities were then repackaged again into more complex products called collateralised debt obligations, or CDOs, and sold to investors around the world.

body.caption: The Subprime Chain: Who Did What, and Who Carried the Risk

cells: Lender, such as New Century Financial
Made the loan, then sold it
Only briefly, until the loan was sold
Bought loans, bundled them into MBS and CDOs
Not by design, though many kept large amounts they could not sell
Fees paid by the issuers of the securities
Global investors: banks, pension funds, mutual funds
Bought the securities for their yield and high ratings
Yes, they held the final risk

body.text: Look at the last column. Almost everyone in the chain earned money on volume, and almost no one who approved or packaged the loan bore the cost of it going bad. When incentives reward the number of loans rather than their quality, quality collapses. That is the single most important cause of the subprime crisis.

body.title: Two Ways to Make a Home Loan

columns.label: Originate to Hold
points: The lender keeps the loan on its own books
It loses money if the borrower defaults
So it checks income, credit history and property value carefully
Loan growth is limited by the lender's own capital
This is still the dominant model for Indian banks and housing finance companies

columns.label: Originate to Distribute
points: The lender sells the loan within weeks
The default risk moves to distant investors
Checks weaken, because volume earns fees
Loan growth is limited only by investor demand for securities
This was the dominant model for US subprime loans in the boom

body.title: Moody's AAA Rated Mortgage Securities From 2006: What Happened to the Ratings

body.label: The Ratings Failure
body.context: Moody's eventually downgraded 83% of the $869 billion of mortgage securities it had rated AAA in 2006. AAA is supposed to mean the safest possible investment.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Pooling thousands of home loans and turning them into bonds that can be sold to investors is called ___.
body.explanation: Securitisation is a legitimate tool that can spread risk and lower borrowing costs. In the subprime boom it was misused: it separated the people making loans from the people bearing the risk, and it hid how weak the underlying loans were behind AAA ratings.

children.text: Leverage on Top of Leverage

The chain was leveraged at every link. A homebuyer who put down 5% was running 20 times leverage on the house: a 5% fall in its price wiped out their equity. The investment banks buying and holding mortgage securities were leveraged too. Lehman Brothers' 2007 annual report showed about $31 of assets for every $1 of shareholders' equity.

body.title: Your Turn: How Thin Was the Cushion?
body.prompt: A bank holds $31 of assets for every $1 of shareholders' equity. By what percentage do its assets need to fall in value to wipe out its equity completely? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Equity is $1 out of $31 of assets, so a fall of $1 wipes it out. $1 divided by $31 is about 3.23%. A bank leveraged 31 to 1 cannot survive even a modest fall in the value of its assets. US home prices eventually fell about 27% from their peak, and the securities built on subprime loans fell far more.

children.text: The Fuse Burns: 2006 to 2007

body.title: From Housing Peak to Global Alarm

events.title: House Prices Peak
events.description: US national house prices top out after roughly doubling. The Fed's rate has reached 5.25%, and teaser rates start resetting higher.

events.title: Defaults Surface
events.description: With prices flat or falling, struggling borrowers can no longer sell or refinance. Subprime defaults climb rapidly.

events.title: A Major Lender Fails
events.description: New Century Financial, once the second largest subprime lender in the US, files for bankruptcy.

events.title: Bear Stearns Funds in Trouble
events.description: Merrill Lynch seizes over $800 million of assets from two Bear Stearns hedge funds that had made highly leveraged bets on subprime securities. Both funds file for bankruptcy on 31 July.

events.title: The Crisis Goes Global
events.description: France's BNP Paribas freezes three funds worth about €1.6 billion, saying it can no longer value their US mortgage-linked assets because liquidity in that market has evaporated. Many date the start of the global crisis to this day.

events.title: The Explosion
events.description: Losses spread to the investment banks at the centre of the chain. Lesson 3.2 picks up the story.

events.title: The Bottom
events.description: US national house prices finally bottom out, about 27% below their 2006 peak, the deepest national fall since the Great Depression.

children.text: Why India's Banks Were Not Holding the Bomb

India did not escape 2008, as Lesson 3.3 will show. But its banks were not sitting on piles of toxic housing loans, and that was partly by design. Under Governor Y.V. Reddy, the Reserve Bank of India leaned against the property boom well before the crisis. It raised the risk weight on housing loans to 75% in 2004, raised the risk weight on commercial real estate exposure to 150% around 2005 to 2006, and increased provisioning on standard loans to real estate, capital markets and personal loans to 2% between 2005 and 2007. Securitisation of home loans also remained a small market in India. In December 2008, the New York Times credited these tough standards with protecting Indian banks from the subprime crisis.

stats.label: Housing Loan Risk Weight, 2004
stats.context: Raised by RBI, so banks had to hold more capital against home loans

stats.label: Teaser Loan Provisioning, 2010
stats.context: Five times the normal 0.4%, discouraging teaser home loans

stats.label: Maximum LTV Today
stats.context: Depending on loan size, so borrowers must put money down

children.text: The teaser loan story is a small but telling example. State Bank of India popularised teaser home loans in India after 2008, with low fixed rates for the first few years. Having watched what teasers did in the US, RBI required banks to set aside 2% provisions on such loans, compared with 0.4% for ordinary loans. SBI withdrew its teaser schemes from 1 May 2011.

body.title: The Too-Good-To-Be-True Home Loan
body.scenario: Arjun, a 29 year old software engineer in Pune earning ₹1.1 lakh a month after tax, is buying a ₹70 lakh flat. A loan agent offers him a package with an attractive starting rate for the first two years that will then move to the lender's floating rate. At the starting rate, the EMI on a ₹56 lakh loan would be about ₹45,000. The agent says: "Do not worry about the later rate, property prices here are rising 12% a year, so you can always sell at a profit or refinance."
body.prompt: Using lessons from the subprime crisis, what questions should Arjun ask, and what calculations should he do before signing?
body.modelAnswer: The agent's pitch repeats the exact reasoning that failed in the US: qualify on the low starting payment and rely on rising prices as the escape route. Arjun should ask what the rate becomes after two years and how the reset is calculated, whether the lender will increase the EMI or extend the tenure, and what prepayment or switching charges apply. He should then stress-test the loan: recalculate the EMI at the expected floating rate and at 2 to 3 percentage points higher, and check what share of his ₹1.1 lakh income that represents. An EMI of ₹45,000 is already about 41% of his take-home pay, so even a moderate increase could push it past half of his income, leaving little room for other expenses or a job loss. He should also test the "prices always rise" assumption: if property prices stayed flat for five years, or fell 10%, could he still afford the loan, and would selling cover the outstanding amount after brokerage and stamp duty costs? Finally, the ₹56 lakh loan is 80% of the ₹70 lakh price, the maximum RBI allows for a loan of that size, so he has no extra cushion. The core lesson from 2008: borrow only what you can repay at a realistically higher rate, from your income, without relying on rising prices.

body.title: Stress-Test Your Own Home Loan
steps: Find your current loan outstanding, interest rate and remaining tenure in your lender's app or latest loan statement
Use the EMI calculator to find your EMI if your rate rises by 2 percentage points, and again by 3 percentage points
Work out what share of your monthly take-home pay each of those EMIs would be
Check whether your lender adjusts the EMI or extends the tenure when rates rise, and how many years a rate rise would add
Check that your loan agreement has no teaser or step-up rate reset you have forgotten about
Estimate your current loan to value: loan outstanding divided by a conservative estimate of the property's value today
Ask yourself: if property prices were flat for five years, would this loan still work for my household?

body.label: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report
body.description: The official US inquiry into the causes of the 2008 crisis. Chapter 5 covers subprime lending in detail, and the graphics library shows how loan quality fell during the boom.

cards.definition: A loan to a borrower who would not qualify for a standard loan, typically due to weak credit or unverified income, at a higher interest rate.
Boom era slang for a loan to a borrower with No Income, No Job and no Assets, made with little or no verification.
A low initial interest rate for the first few years of a loan, after which the rate resets higher.
Pooling loans and turning them into tradable securities sold to investors.
A bond backed by a pool of home loans, paying investors from borrowers' EMIs.
A lending model where loans are made to be sold on, so the lender earns fees without bearing long-term default risk.
The loan amount divided by the property's value. RBI caps it at 75% to 90% for home loans, depending on loan size.
A regulatory multiplier that decides how much capital a bank must hold against a loan. Higher risk weights make risky lending more expensive for banks.

points: By 2006, subprime loans made up about 23.5% of US mortgage originations, many with no income checks, little down payment and teaser rates
A 1% Fed rate and rising house prices hid weak loans, because struggling borrowers could always sell or refinance while prices rose
Teaser resets are brutal: on a ₹40 lakh, 20 year loan, moving from 7.5% to 10.5% raises the EMI by about 24%
Securitisation separated the people making loans from the people bearing the risk, and AAA ratings hid the danger, with Moody's later cutting 83% of its 2006 AAA mortgage ratings
Leverage ran through the whole chain: at 31 to 1, a fall of just 3.2% in asset values wipes out a bank's equity
RBI's higher risk weights, extra provisioning, LTV caps and discouragement of teaser loans helped keep Indian banks away from the subprime bomb

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment or lending advice. EMI figures are illustrative calculations and actual loan terms vary by lender. Regulatory limits such as LTV caps, risk weights and provisioning norms reflect the position understood at the time of writing and can change.
